3396.tone: Aceto 2004: 487-488 (= 2008 c. 296-297), reporting Sutcliffe 2003 (Bajan data from Roberts 1988: 94), describes lexically contrastive pitch patterns on disyllables shared by Bajan and Guyanese (sister / - _ / 'female sibling' vs sistér / _ - / 'nun'; múhda 'mother' vs mùhdá 'female head of a religious order'; fáada 'father' vs fàadá 'priest'; brúhda vs brùhdá; fárma 'one who farms' vs fàrmá surname; béeka vs bèeká surname) and calls it lexical tone ('This feature has not been attested for other Caribbean creoles'); he adds that Sutcliffe also treats downstepping, final cadence, final rise, high rise intonation, emphasis and focus marking. Sutcliffe 2003 (excerpt) states that word stress is assigned independently of tone, tone being 'entered into the lexicon, and attached to... mora'. So the source describes a stress system (lexical, English-type) with a lexical pitch/tone overlay, not a tone system in place of stress. Alternative coding if the pitch overlay is taken as primary: tone or pitch accent. Blake's own Bajan chapter (2004: 504) says only that CECs keep unreduced vowels in unstressed syllables (syllable-timed impression) and use a broad pitch range.

tn.translation: In Bakwé there are three tone levels, called high, mid and low. The high tone is marked by an apostrophe at the beginning of the word. ... The mid tone is pronounced at a medium pitch. Being neither high nor low, it is not marked by a tone sign. ... The low tone is marked by a hyphen at the beginning of the word. ... If the word is longer, it consists of two, three, four or even more syllables, each of which carries at least one tone. ... When a syllable carries two or three different tones, its vowel becomes long. The vowel is then written two or three times.

3405.dq: il existe en banda un accent d'intensité qui affecte certaines syllabes des mots, en sorte que les syllabes non accentuées s'abrègent et ont une tendance à disparaître
3405.dloc: Phonétique, section 'ACCENT.', pp. 23-24 (Google Books scan H1cOAAAAYAAJ)
3405.prule: No stress position is stated. Word prosody is described as three lexical tone levels (haut, moyen, bas: 'la langue banda est chantée'); besides the pitch accent the grammar recognises an 'accent d'intensité' on 'certaines syllabes des mots' whose only stated correlate is the shortening and loss of unaccented syllables (Bĕleda > bleda, temŏ > tem, marœ > mar). The three examples reduce an initial syllable once and a final syllable twice, so no positional or weight rule can be read off.
3405.quote: ACCENT. La langue banda est chantée, c'est-à-dire, que chaque syllabe a sa tonalité propre, et est prononcée sur un ton plus élevé ou plus bas que la voisine. En dehors de l'accent de hauteur, il existe en banda un accent d'intensité qui affecte certaines syllabes des mots, en sorte que les syllabes non accentuées s'abrègent et…
3405.loc: Phonétique, section 'ACCENT.', pp. 23-24 (Google Books scan H1cOAAAAYAAJ)
3405.idn: Tisserant 1930 describes 'banda' as one language: p. 4 '1. Dialecte banda' lists Banda (Banda-Banda) alongside Linda, Gbwende, Moruba, Togbo, Ngura, Ka, Ndi, Gbaga, Mbi and some twenty other tribes, and the ACCENT section (pp. 23-24) speaks only of 'banda' without naming a variety. The tone/intensity-accent statement…
3405.tone: Three lexical tone levels (high nó, dí, ká 'tout'; mid enji 'ils'; low mbwạnga 'palabre'); tone is written only where syntactic function changes it (the verbal noun raises the verb's vowel tone: tee fu'fu vs tee fu wa; loban ge'gere vs loban gere wa). Footnote 3 (pp. 23-24) shows the language spoken on the drum by striking the tone series 1/2/3 of each syllable; its line 'Les mots étrangers... reçoivent leurs accents tout comme les mots banda authentiques' refers to those drum tones ('même série d'accents'), not to the intensity accent. Separately from tone, an 'accent d'intensité' exists on certain syllables of the word, position unstated; p. 19 adds that œ is 'fréquent en banda, surtout dans des syllabes peu accentuées' (vowel reduction in weak syllables).

3407.dq: Stress is noncontrastive on the word level; it is governed by tone and word shape. ... The stress can be perturbed in the context of a longer utterance, but this has not been studied in detail.
3407.dloc: sec. 5.2 'Stress', p. 144; tone inventory sec. 3.1, p. 141; dialect and fieldwork site sec. 0, p. 134
3407.prule: Five-tone language (H, M, L, Falling, Rising; every syllable bears a tone; tone lexical in all word classes and grammatical in verbs and pronouns). Stress is explicitly non-contrastive at word level and is only a phonetic amplitude difference 'governed by tone and word shape': in disyllables both syllables are stressed equally whatever the tones; in trisyllables the penult is usually the weakest of the three (initial and final stronger), unless the penult carries the word's only high tone, in which case it takes more stress. No positional stress rule independent of tone is stated; words of four or more syllables are not described for stress.
3407.srule: Not mentioned in Sampson 1985 (OPSL 4), sec. 5.2 'Stress' p. 144 and secs. 3-8 pp. 141-147 read: the source ranks no stressed syllable over another (disyllables equally stressed; trisyllables first and last stronger than the penult unless the penult bears the only H tone), so no primary/secondary distinction exists to report.
3407.quote: 5.2. Stress. Stress is noncontrastive on the word level; it is governed by tone and word shape. Phonetically, stress is only a greater degree of amplitude relative to unstressed syllables. In two-syllable words, each syllable is stressed equally, regardless of tone. In three-syllable words, the penultimate syllable usually takes less stress than the other two, but will take more stress if it carries the only high tone in the word. The stress can be perturbed in the context of a longer utterance, but this has not been studied in detail. ... 3.1. Inventory and Description. There are five emic t…
3407.loc: sec. 5.2 'Stress', p. 144; tone inventory sec. 3.1, p. 141; dialect and fieldwork site sec. 0, p. 134
3407.idn: Source describes the Tangbago dialect of Banda (Glottolog tang1341, a dialect under band1345 Banda-Ndélé), as recorded at Sopo, Bahr el Ghazal, Sudan, October 1981 - March 1983; Sampson notes Tangbago is one of the largest Banda dialects in Sudan and also a major dialect in CAR.
3407.exq_: In three-syllable words, the penultimate syllable usually takes less stress than the other two, but will take more stress if it carries the only high tone in the word. The stress can be perturbed in the context of a longer utterance, but this has not been studied in detail.
3407.tone: Five emic tones (H, M, L, Falling, Rising), all five on CV syllables, only H/M/L on V syllables (sec. 3.2.1, p. 141); the SAL Supplement 9 version of the same description (sec. 3.3, p. 271) states tone is lexical in all word classes and grammatical in verbs and pronouns. 'Stress' exists only as non-contrastive amplitude governed by tone and word shape; in trisyllables a penult bearing the word's only H tone attracts the stress, i.e. prominence follows tone rather than a fixed position.

In the corresponding affirmative forms it carries a floating tone (LH for the unrealisable conditional, L for the imperative/optative). tn.quote: Le bangubangu a un système tonal à deux tons: Haut (H) et Bas (B). Les verbes sont divisés en deux classes tonales: verbes à ton H et verbes à ton B. … Les noms à deux syllabes en bangubangu ont quatre mélodies: B, BH, HB et H. Comme dans le cas des verbes, le ton des noms se déplace d’une syllabe à droite. Un ton B par défaut remplace le ton qui s’est déplacé. Tout préfixe ayant une voyelle prend un ton B par défaut, mais le préfixe nasal de la classe 10 n’est pas syllabique et ne prend pas de ton.
tn.translation: Bangubangu has a tonal system with two tones: High (H) and Low (B). Verbs are divided into two tone classes: H-tone verbs and B-tone verbs. ... Two-syllable nouns in Bangubangu have four melodies: B, BH, HB and H. As with verbs, the tone of nouns shifts one syllable to the right. A default B tone replaces the tone that has shifted. Every prefix with a vowel takes a default B tone, but the class 10 nasal prefix is not syllabic and takes no tone.

The grammar thus posits, beside the tones it marks (§19 Tonzeichen, §20 Tonlehre), a word-level dynamic (stress) accent that always falls on the stem syllable and is therefore left unmarked; the statement carries no examples, no mea…

3412.tone: Five tonemes (bas `, moyen -, haut ´, montant ˇ, descendant ˆ), pp. 14-15. The only mention of 'accent' in the whole thesis (a full-text search of: one hit, 'accentuée', p. 75) concerns the rare H-B melody on disyllables, which the author attributes to English initial stress in loanwords, p. 75: 'D'une manière générale la succession H-B se retrouve sur les mots empruntés à la langue anglaise. Ex: ɓótà "beurre" de l'anglais "butter" / sóndʒà "policier" "soldier" / drósì "caleçon" "dress" / kótì "jaquette courte" "coatee" / kótìn "coton" "cotton"... Cette structure H-B pourrait donc être expliquée par le fait que pour la majorité de ces mots anglais la 1ère syllabe est mise en valeur par un accent... Malgré l'origine de cette structure, nous avons rencontré quelques mots de la langue bàŋkón qui portent la séquence H-B.... Mais, ces unités ne sont pas nombreuses. Environ 6/1400.' (The typescript alternates ɓ and plain b in the language name: p. 13 and the first p. 14 instance carry the hooked ɓ, the second p. 14 instance and the p. 75 line carry plain b; each quotation follows its own line.) The source neither asserts nor denies a native word accent. Atindogbé 2007 (ASM 28(4): 157, saved) simplifies to two tones: 'Bankon has two tones: low and high... Both combine to produce two contour tones: falling and rising'; Hyman & Lionnet 2011 analyse Abo as an H/L tone language with verb-final metatony; neither mentions stress or accent (a full-text search of full text: 0 hits).

tn.quote: Grâce à ces oppostions en CI, nous avons pu prouver que les cinq tons inventoriés assurent une fonction distinctive en bàŋkón. Ce sont désormais des tonèmes. ... Au total cinq tons: *trois tons ponctuels, ou registres (3 niveaux pertinents): - le ton ponctuel haut (´) - le ton ponctuel moyen (-) - le ton ponctuel bas (`) *deux tons modulés: - le ton haut-bas ou descendant (ˆ) - le ton bas-haut ou montant (ˇ) ... nous pouvons oser affirmer que le ɓàŋkón est une langue à registres qui combinent deux tons modulés pouvant être analysés chacun en une succession de deux tons ponctuels.
tn.translation: Thanks to these oppositions in identical context, we have been able to prove that the five tones inventoried serve a distinctive function in Bankon. They are henceforth tonemes. ... In all five tones: *three punctual (level) tones, or registers (3 relevant levels): the high, mid and low level tones; *two modulated tones: the high-low or falling tone, the low-high or rising tone ... we can venture to state that Bankon is a register language which combines two modulated tones, each analysable as a succession of two level tones.

3414.dq: 1. On 2-syllabled words. Stress is usually on last syllable ... 2. On 3-syllabled words. Stress is usually on third syllable. ... 3. On words of more than 3 syllables. Stress is usually on the last two syllables.
3414.dloc: Southwell 1990 reprint p. 467 (archive.org item KayanEnglishDictionary, text p. 251, right-hand page), section 'C. Additional non-segmental phonetic phenomena', 'a. Non-phonemic', 'Stress', items 1-3.
3414.prule: Non-phonemic word stress at the right edge, quantity-insensitive and computable from syllable count: 2-syllable words are 'usually' stressed on the last syllable; 3-syllable words 'usually' on the third (final) syllable; words of more than 3 syllables 'usually' on the last two syllables (penult and final both marked, no primary/secondary distinction). Level ('even') stress on both syllables or fluctuation between first and second syllable is a minority variant in disyllables; second+third 'occasionally' and first+third 'rarely' in trisyllables.
3414.srule: No primary/secondary ranking in the source: Cubit 1964 describes unranked double stress -- words of more than three syllables are 'usually' stressed on both of the last two syllables (penult + final, e.g. (pələ'mɑ'nʌ) 'to consider'); 3-syllable words 'occasionally' on second+third, 'rarely' first+third; 2-syllable words 'occasionally' even on both. No alternating/rhythmic secondary stress described; words have at most five syllables (p. 468). [Clayre & Cubit 1974: 477 instead give even stress on penult+final for three- and four-syllable words and 'usually even stress' in disyllables.]
3414.quote: C. ADDITIONAL NON-SEGMENTAL PHONETIC PHENOMENA a. Non-phonemic Stress 1. On 2-syllabled words. Stress is usually on last syllable but occasionally may be even on both syllables or may fluctuate between first and second syllable. (an'a:k) child 2. On 3-syllabled words. Stress is usually on third syllable. May occasionally be on second and third or rarely on first and third. (bəku'lɔ') wild cat 3. On words of more than 3 syllables. Stress is usually on the last two syllables. (pələ'mɑ'nʌ) to consider

3416.dq: Two important aspects of Bardi prosody are a stress system consisting of independent primary and secondary stress assignments, and an intonational system. The intonation system consists of boundary tones and pitch accents that interact with the stress system. [...] Primary stress is regular and appears consistently on the initial syllable of the word.

3416.heavy: (primary stress is quantity-insensitive; weight governs only secondary stress) 'A light syllable is an open syllable with a short vowel; syllables with codas and long vowels are heavy.' (p. 343)
3416.dflt: Primary stress is always word-initial; when the final syllable is light the weight-conditioned secondary stress falls on the penult (tetrasyllables and longer), and disyllables / underlying trisyllables carry the initial primary only.
3416.prule: Primary stress is fixed on the initial syllable of every word (left edge), regardless of syllable weight or word length; it is demarcative ('regular', 'consistently', 'predictable'), not lexical and not a pitch-accent system. Cues: longer duration, greater intensity, sometimes higher pitch (the H* pitch accent of the intonation system aligns to the primary-stressed initial syllable of content words, p. 345, 347).
3416.srule: Secondary stress (independent of the fixed initial primary stress) is weight- and morphology-sensitive (heavy = closed syllable or long vowel). Morphologically simple words: disyllables and underlyingly trisyllabic words have none; trisyllables derived by final-vowel deletion stress the (heavy) third syllable; tetrasyllables stress the third syllable if the fourth is light, the fourth if it is heavy; further secondary stresses fall on a final heavy syllable or else the penult, then alternate left to right (underived examples rare). Verb roots carry stress on their first syllable; heavy case markers (-nim, -ngan), heavy monosyllabic clitics (=jin, =min) and agreement clitics take secondary stress, which can break the alternation and produce clash, with speaker variation (ex. 4a-c). E.g. /ˈmiliˌmili/, /ˈpilaŋkaˌmar/, /ˈpiliŋˌpiliŋˌkun/, /ˈcawurkaˌwurka/.

Three and four syllable word stems exemplify the stress pattern of an iamb. Stress is consistently assigned to the second syllable: CV.CV́.CV. ... Words of four syllables and more exhibit primary and secondary stress. A few nouns fit this description; many inflected verbs do als…
3420.dloc: pp. 8-9, section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)', Farr & Farr 2005
3420.heavy: Heterogeneous vowel clusters (all 20 combinations): 'These vowel sequences function as the bi-moraic nucleus of one heavy syllable. We prefer the term complex vowel nucleus rather than diphthong... As heavy syllables, they usually draw stress to themselves.' (p. 4). Geminate (lengthened) vowels VV: 'They tend to draw stress to themselves.' (p. 7) 'When a lengthened vowel occurs in the same word with a heterogeneous vowel sequence, the syllable with the long vowel often has primary stress, so geminate vowels pattern as more heavy than heterogeneous vowel sequences.' (p. 8). Syllable patterns are V, VV, CV, CVV only (p. 11), so no coda weight exists.
3420.dflt: Disyllables: initial ((C)V́.CV, e.g. mé.ndi 'boy'); three- and four-syllable stems: second syllable (CV.CV́.CV, a.rí.ri, e.vé.tu, e.vé.ve.tu, di.dí.vu.gè); i.e. grids 10 010 0100 for light-only words; words of 4+ syllables add secondary stress (a.yó.bo.rò, ta.tá.fu.gè); some long inflected verbs show a different primary (ni.nì.ngi.gu.tá.re, primary on the penult) which the source does not explain
3420.prule: Weight-sensitive default with lexical residue: a heavy syllable (complex vowel nucleus CVV or geminate VV; only open syllables exist) attracts primary stress wherever it stands (ga.ndáu, táu.ba.na, a.kúa.go); with two heavies the first (or the geminate-vowel one) wins. Light-only words take a count-dependent default: initial in disyllables ((C)V́.CV), second syllable in three- and four-syllable stems (CV.CV́.CV, 'iamb'); 4+ syllable words add secondary stress. Predictable for ~95% of the lexicon.
3420.srule: Stated, placement not given as a rule: 'Words of four syllables and more exhibit primary and secondary stress' (a few nouns, many inflected verbs); secondary is marked with a grave only in this section, and the marked examples place it on alternate syllables to the right of the second-syllable primary (a.yó.bo.rò, ta.tá.fu.gè, di.dí.vu.gè, bu.bú.bu.gù.tu.rè.re), with one inflected verb showing a secondary on the 2nd syllable before a penultimate primary (ni.nì.ngi.gu.tá.re, unexplained). Compounds: secondary stress on the initial syllable of the second constituent (áiro-àiro, méne-mène), except jója-tófo with two primaries (p. 14).
3420.quote: Stress is predictable for about 95% of the lexicon. For two syllable words, the default stress pattern is: (C)V́.CV: <mé.ndi> ‘boy’ ... A heavy syllable tends to pull stress to it, so CV.CV́V is stressed on the second syllable. 3420.lexex: Lexical residue (~5%): final-stressed disyllables (C)V.CV́, mostly functors (a.mó 'I/me', i.ngá, a.ná, ko.tú 'and', a.tá, ta.gó) but some nominals (fi.rí 'flesh', ra.gá, du.ró, du.rá, go.mbú, tu.mbó 'yesterday', go.só 'cloud'), with minimal pairs (a.gha 'cup' / a.ghá 'thus'; a.ji / a.jí; e.gha / e.ghá; u.ndu / u.ndú; u.va / u.vá 'liver'; bu.rú.ru ea / bú.ru.ru ea); and four trisyllables that follow neither the default CV.CV́.CV pattern nor the heavy-syllable rule: initial-stressed nó.mo.no 'cross-cousin', é.ni.ma (in é.ni.ma yó.yo) and ná.ma.ne 'we.EXC', plus vai.kí.na 'Palm Cockatoo', stressed on the second syllable although its heavy initial syllable <vai> should have drawn the stress (p. 10). Exceptional stress is written with an acute in the practical orthography (p. 14).

3420.exq_: Stress is predictable for about 95% of the lexicon. (p. 8) ... There are several (C)V.CV́ words in Tafota Baruga. Some are even minimal pairs with those having the default stress pattern: (C)V́.CV. ... Many words with the (C)V.CV́ stress pattern are functors: <a.mó> ‘I/me’ <i.ngá> ‘the two of you’ …
3420.tone: No tone is described for Tafota Baruga (section headed 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)'); vowel length and nasality are phonemic (p. 8). Smallhorn 2011:79 reports tone for Suena (Wilson 1974) and Binandere (Wilson 1992) and lists Baruga, with Yekora and Korafe, under 'Phonemic stress with a low functional load'. For tone the entry now rests on Farr & Farr n.d., quoted in the tone block.

tn.quote: Baruga words are stress-timed, with longer words pronounced in approximately the same time as shorter words. Primary stress within a word is associated with a 'heavy' syllable such as bee 'truth', a syllable which is uttered for a longer duration than the other syllables in the word. A heavy syllable may also manifest increased amplitude and a higher pitch. Stress is predictable for many of the words in Baruga. … Where stress is not predictable, an acute accent (e.g. á) is written over the most sonorous vowel in the stressed syllable.

tn.note: Nothing on lexical tone; pitch is mentioned only as a possible correlate of the stressed heavy syllable and as rising intonation in polar questions. Acute accents in the forms mark stress, not tone.

3420.cfw: Farr and Farr's 2005 phonology sketch, the only first-hand description of Tafota Baruga, states a clear weight-sensitive rule (initial stress in disyllables, second syllable in three- and four-syllable stems, heavy syllables attracting stress, about five percent lexical exceptions), and Smallhorn's 2011 comparative study, which takes its Baruga stress data from Farr and Farr, is consistent with it, but no second independent description exists.
